channel.title: Curated Travel Magazine
channel.description: Travel reporting, cultural heritage, and responsible exploration worldwide.

item.title: Karijini National Park Adds New Access to the Dramatic Knox Gorge
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Western Australia’s Karijini National Park has received a $2.1 million infrastructure upgrade, improving access to one of its most spectacular areas. At Knox Gorge, visitors can now make use of a raised steel boardwalk and new accessible path leading to the gorge lookout, along with an expanded car park, new toilet facilities and upgraded picnic areas.

Known for its rugged red-rock landscapes, deep gorges, rock pools and waterfalls, Karijini offers a dramatically different side of Western Australia from the beaches and vineyards associated with Perth and the southwest. The improvements make it easier for more visitors to experience the landscape while enhancing facilities in a region where the wilderness remains the primary attraction.

The Curated Take:
The most interesting part of the investment may be its balance between access and landscape. Better infrastructure can make a remote natural attraction more approachable without taking away the reason travelers came in the first place: the feeling of entering a vast, otherworldly Australian wilderness.

item.title: Margaret River Winery Earns a Perfect 100 Points
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Margaret River has reached a milestone for Western Australian wine, with House of Cards’ Ace High Chardonnay 2025 receiving the region’s first perfect 100-point score for a still wine from the International Wine & Spirit Competition. The achievement came during the IWSC Global Tasting in Margaret River, where wines from the region collected an impressive 29 Gold medals. House of Cards also earned 98 points for its The Royals Chardonnay 2025 and 95 for its Kings in the Corner Cabernet Merlot 2024, along with the 2026 IWSC Western Australian Wine Producer Trophy.

The recognition puts Margaret River’s celebrated wine scene firmly in the international spotlight while highlighting the breadth of producers working across the region. For travelers, it offers another reason to look beyond the cellar door and explore the vineyards, restaurants and landscapes that have made Margaret River one of Australia’s most distinctive wine destinations.

The Curated Take:
A perfect score is attention-grabbing, but the larger story is what it says about Margaret River’s place in the global wine conversation. The combination of acclaimed Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon and an established cellar-door culture makes this a region worth exploring as a complete food-and-wine destination rather than simply stopping at one celebrated producer.

item.title: Jacada Travel Expands Positive Impact Collection with 39 Purpose-Driven Experiences
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Luxury travel specialist Jacada Travel has added 39 new experiences to its Positive Impact Collection, bringing together immersive encounters designed to benefit local communities, protect ecosystems, preserve cultural heritage and support wildlife conservation. Each experience has been assessed against the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and Jacada’s own Positive Impact Principles, with an emphasis on meaningful exchange rather than superficial sightseeing.

The new additions span five themes: upcycling and circular economies, female leadership and Indigenous stewardship, community-led wildlife protection, regenerative foodways, and the preservation of living mastercraft. Travelers can transform confiscated poaching snares into jewelry in Zambia and Zimbabwe, explore a women-led cacao ritual with Costa Rica’s BriBri community, visit Kenya’s Indigenous-owned Reteti Elephant Sanctuary, participate in marine conservation in Mozambique, forage for coastal ingredients in Ireland, or learn traditional weaving techniques in Japan. Other experiences include climate-smart farming in Zimbabwe, turtle hatchling releases in Vietnam, artisan workshops with disabled craftspeople in Tanzania, and tree planting in Bhutan.

The Curated Take

Jacada’s expanded collection reflects a more thoughtful direction for luxury travel, one in which access and comfort are paired with accountability. The most compelling experiences are those that allow travelers to see how conservation, cultural continuity and economic resilience are connected. Whether learning how discarded materials become valuable crafts or discovering how tourism can support former poachers and local women-led enterprises, these encounters offer a deeper understanding of place while directing attention and resources toward locally defined priorities.

item.title: Bloom Festival Celebrates Western Australia’s Spring Wildflower Season
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
From wildflower walks through mountain ranges to botanical workshops, Aboriginal cultural experiences and long-table food and wine events, Western Australia’s Great Southern region is welcoming spring with the return of Bloom Festival, running September 12 through October 11, 2026. Spanning destinations from Kojonup to Bremer Bay, including Denmark and Albany/Kinjarling, the annual celebration brings together the region’s natural landscapes, local producers, artists and communities.

The festival offers a varied way to experience the Great Southern at one of its most colorful times of year. Visitors can explore markets featuring local produce and handmade crafts, join guided walks and tours, discover visual art and craft exhibitions, or enjoy live music and family-focused activities. With the Stirling and Porongurup Ranges providing a dramatic backdrop, Bloom presents the region not simply as a place to see wildflowers, but as a destination where nature, culture and local creativity intersect.

The Curated Take:
Bloom Festival offers a more layered approach to spring travel than a simple wildflower-viewing excursion. The combination of guided landscape experiences, Aboriginal cultural tours, regional food and art gives visitors multiple ways to connect with the Great Southern, making the season an invitation to explore the character of the region as much as its scenery.

item.title: Plein Air Down Under Turns the Peel Region Into a 300-Kilometre Art Trail
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
More than 200 artists will spread across Western Australia’s Peel region this September for Plein Air Down Under, Australia’s largest outdoor painting festival. Taking place September 22–29, the event invites artists to paint the region’s waterways, coastline and heritage streetscapes in the open air, transforming the landscape itself into a temporary gallery. Visitors can watch artists work, attend demonstrations and participate in art activities alongside live music.

The festival offers an unusually intimate way to experience Mandurah/Mandjoogoordap and the wider Peel region, shifting attention from conventional sightseeing toward observation and creativity. Rather than viewing the destination through a camera lens alone, visitors can see how artists interpret the same landscapes in real time.

The Curated Take:
Plein air painting encourages a slower way of seeing a destination. For travelers, the attraction isn’t only the finished art but watching artists respond to the light, water, architecture and atmosphere of the Peel in real time. It turns a regional landscape into both subject and experience.

item.title: Noongar Storytelling Takes Over Perth’s Swan River With Story of Kooyar
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Ancient Noongar storytelling will take center stage along Perth’s Elizabeth Quay and the Derbal Yerrigan/Swan River this September with Story of Kooyar, an immersive production combining light, water and sound. Running September 25–28, the 20-minute projection follows Kooyar, the frog, through the Noongar six seasons as he helps restore and heal Boordja, or Country. The experience unfolds on a water screen emerging from the river, accompanied by roving Karak puppets and live performances from Indigenous dance group Corroboree For Life.

The production offers visitors a nighttime cultural experience rooted in the stories and seasonal understanding of the Noongar people. By using the Swan River itself as part of the stage, Story of Kooyar creates an experience in which place and storytelling are closely connected rather than presenting Indigenous culture as something separate from the landscape.

The Curated Take:
This is the kind of cultural experience that can change how a traveler sees a familiar city. Instead of simply presenting a performance, Story of Kooyar uses Perth’s river and night sky as part of the storytelling, connecting contemporary technology with an ancient relationship to Country.

item.title: SAKA Museum Traces the Living Tradition of Kamasan Painting in Its First Temporary Exhibition
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
SAKA Museum at AYANA Bali has opened its first temporary exhibition with KAMASAN: The Noble Tradition of Balinese Painting, an expansive look at one of Bali’s most distinctive artistic traditions. Running through May 30, 2027, the exhibition brings together more than 30 works spanning the late 19th century to today, including ritual cloths, palm-leaf works, an astrological calendar and paintings preserved by the families of Kamasan masters. Rooted in the village of Kamasan and closely connected to Balinese-Hindu ritual, the tradition is recognizable for its highly codified figures, elaborate linework and connection to the visual language of wayang kulit.

Rather than treating Kamasan as a historical art form frozen in time, the exhibition places classical works alongside contemporary artists who are pushing its visual vocabulary into new territory. Curated by Farah Wardani and Made Chandra, the exhibition explores hereditary master painters, the women who have sustained the tradition, and a younger generation using Kamasan imagery to consider identity, ecology, technology and collective memory. The result is a portrait of a tradition that has survived not by remaining unchanged, but by continually finding ways to speak to the present.

The Curated Take:
KAMASAN offers a particularly meaningful way to encounter Balinese culture because the paintings are inseparable from the beliefs, rituals, stories and communities that shaped them. The decision to give contemporary practitioners equal footing with historic works also makes this more than a survey of traditional art. It invites visitors to consider what cultural preservation actually looks like when a living tradition is allowed to evolve.

item.title: Mulia Bali’s “A Night in Elysium” Brings a Grand Finale to the 2026 Festive Season
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Mulia Bali is turning the holiday season into a full resort experience, with Christmas celebrations, family programming, festive dining and a lavish New Year’s Eve finale planned for 2026. Set along the shores of Nusa Dua, the resort’s festivities culminate December 31 with “A Night in Elysium,” a gala in the Grand Ballroom featuring international performers, elaborate dining and a midnight countdown designed to carry the celebration into 2027.

The evening’s entertainment brings together The Starlets, whose performers have appeared at major international events and in West End productions including Hamilton and TINA – The Tina Turner Musical, with Australian live band Fiction. Across the wider festive calendar, guests can choose from Christmas Eve and Christmas Day feasts, countdown dinners at the resort’s restaurants and a kids program of creative workshops and holiday activities. Family packages, breakfast-inclusive direct-booking benefits and a dining gift-card promotion add further incentives for a holiday stay.

The Curated Take:
For travelers looking to make the holiday season an actual destination experience rather than simply a change of scenery, Bali offers an appealing combination of tropical surroundings and traditional year-end celebration. Mulia’s program is particularly geared toward multigenerational travelers, pairing a substantial entertainment lineup and gala atmosphere with dedicated children’s programming and multiple dining options.

item.title: Grupo Lomas Celebrates 45 Years by Putting Travel Advisors at the Heart of Its Story
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For 45 years, Grupo Lomas has built its presence in Mexico alongside the travel professionals who have connected generations of travelers with the Mexican Caribbean. That relationship took center stage during Lomas Appreciation Week (LAW) 2026, which brought 178 travel advisors together with tour operators from across North America, South America, the United Kingdom and Europe. The gathering also marked the first participation of MICE professionals and saw increased representation from Mexican advisors, reflecting the changing breadth of the travel industry and Grupo Lomas’ advisor community.

Held primarily at El Dorado Royale, the week offered attendees a behind-the-scenes look at the group’s hospitality portfolio, from gastronomy and beach experiences to family-focused entertainment at Nickelodeon Hotels & Resorts Riviera Maya. The program combined business updates and professional development with distinctly Mexican experiences, including the Legacy 45 Gastronomic Market and a playful Super Sliming at Aqua Nick. The week concluded with the LAW Awards, recognizing travel professionals across sales, specialization and wedding travel, while special honors highlighted relationships that have stretched across different stages of Grupo Lomas’ 45-year history.

The Curated Take:
For an industry built on relationships, LAW offers a useful reminder that the travel advisor remains an important part of how destinations and hospitality brands reach travelers. What makes the gathering particularly interesting is its blend of recognition and immersion: advisors aren’t simply being thanked for selling the product, they are being invited to experience the people, food, properties and experiences they ultimately recommend to their clients.

item.title: ANA Makes Perth More Accessible From Tokyo With Daily Flights
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Travel between Japan and Western Australia is about to become considerably easier, with All Nippon Airways increasing its direct Tokyo-Perth service from three flights per week to daily operations beginning October 25, 2026. The expanded schedule will run through March 27, 2027, responding to growing visitor demand from Japan and strengthening one of the key international air links into Western Australia.

The additional frequency is significant for a destination as geographically removed from many of its international markets as Western Australia. Perth now sits at the end of a network of 22 nonstop international routes, giving travelers from Japan and beyond more flexibility when planning a visit to experience the state’s wine regions, coastlines, wilderness and increasingly sophisticated cultural scene.

The Curated Take:
For a destination where distance has historically been part of the allure and the challenge, air connectivity matters. Daily Tokyo service makes Western Australia easier to incorporate into a Japan-Australia itinerary and gives Japanese travelers greater flexibility to explore beyond Australia’s more familiar eastern cities.
